title: Tyson Foods, Inc. v. Commissioner
subject: Substantiation of Deductions and the Cohan Rule
summary: Tyson Foods, Inc. v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2007-188, is a U.S. Tax Court decision holding that Tyson failed to substantiate $2,007,640 in claimed deductions because it produced only a vendor list and no invoices. For corporate taxpayers claiming federal R&D tax credits, it shows the Cohan estimation rule cannot rescue claims lacking contemporaneous records under I.R.C. § 6001.
metaDescription: Tyson Foods v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2007-188: a vendor list and no invoices failed to substantiate $2,007,640 of deductions; Cohan did not help.

body.text: Section 1: Executive Summary & Case Background
Procedural Posture and Factual Genesis of the Dispute

In Tyson Foods, Inc. & Subsidiaries v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2007-188 (Docket No. 21590-03, filed July 16, 2007), the United States Tax Court addressed a critical threshold question of federal tax controversy: the extent to which a sophisticated corporate taxpayer may rely upon judicial estimation under the doctrine of Cohan v. Commissioner, 39 F.2d 540 (2d Cir. 1930), when it fails to maintain contemporaneous source records required by Internal Revenue Code (I.R.C.) § 6001. The petitioner, Tyson Foods, Inc. and Subsidiaries (Tyson), was, during the years in issue, the world's largest fully integrated producer, processor, and marketer of poultry-based food products, headquartered in Springdale, Arkansas, and incorporated in Delaware. Following an examination of Tyson's consolidated federal income tax returns for multiple taxable years in the mid-1990s, the Commissioner of Internal Revenue (Respondent) determined deficiencies of $7,352,495, $2,802,710, and $1,793,801 in Tyson's Federal income taxes for its fiscal years ended September 30, 1995, 1996, and 1997, respectively.

The procedural posture of Docket No. 21590-03 reflects the complex, multi-issue nature of large-case corporate audits conducted by the Internal Revenue Service (IRS). The statutory notice set forth ten separate adjustments, and Tyson raised a new issue in its petition; prior to trial, the parties settled seven issues, two further issues were settled after trial, and one major substantive dispute—the qualification and quantification of Tyson's research and development (R&D) tax credit claim under I.R.C. § 41—was deferred for later trial or other disposition. Consequently, the July 16, 2007 Memorandum Opinion authored by Judge Mary Ann Cohen focused squarely on an evidentiary and substantiation dispute arising from Tyson's August 1994 stock acquisition (treated as an asset purchase for Federal income tax purposes) of Culinary Foods, Inc. (Culinary), a Chicago-based manufacturer of frozen food products for institutional buyers and of other food products for the airline industry, and more specifically from the accounting for a $5 million tax increment financing (TIF) subsidy that the City of Chicago had granted to Culinary.

By the end of 1991, Culinary operated through two integrated manufacturing facilities on the north side of Chicago; in 1992 a fire destroyed one of them, and Culinary temporarily leased two facilities and fitted them out with new machinery; in 1993 it broke ground on a 125,000-square-foot, $18 million office and manufacturing facility in the Back-of-the-Yards neighborhood on the south side of Chicago, in connection with which the City of Chicago granted it, in June 1994, a $5 million TIF subsidy payable over time; and beginning in mid-1995, after the acquisition by Tyson, Culinary moved its operations into the new facility. At the acquisition, Tyson allocated no part of its purchase price to the TIF subsidy receivable (an allocation of $5 million to that receivable was agreed with Respondent only on July 12, 1999, during the audit), and when the City of Chicago paid the subsidy, Tyson did not credit a receivable but instead credited the six payments to various accounts, including account No. 101226, TIF moving expenses, which received check B (dated March 10, 1995), check C (No. 96878721, dated July 5, 1995, for $52,189.43), and check D (dated November 24, 1995). Because these misapplied subsidy credits erroneously increased or decreased Tyson's taxable income, Respondent conceded that Tyson's income should be reduced by $1,800,354 of the misapplied $5 million subsidy, while Tyson contended that it was entitled to deduct an additional $2,007,640 in respect of expenditures debited to account No. 101226 and conceded that it was not entitled to reduce its income by the remaining $1,192,006. The only records explaining the amounts debited to account No. 101226 were lists showing a breakdown by vendor or other brief description, which did not identify the nature of the items or the dates on which the amounts were expended, and no invoices were in the record or ever produced.
The Taxpayer's Claim and the Commissioner's Challenge

Before the Tax Court, Tyson acknowledged that complete and correct records had not been maintained for the disputed Culinary expenditures and contended that its records were insufficient to determine the extent to which these expenses should have reduced otherwise allowable ordinary and necessary business expenses as contrasted with otherwise allowable depreciation, but that, at a minimum, under the well-established rule of Cohan v. Commissioner, it was entitled to treat the entire $2,007,640 as a capital expenditure depreciable over a five-year period and to reduce its taxable income by the resulting additional depreciation deductions. In support, Tyson relied on the list of vendors and amounts recorded in account No. 101226, which it characterized as a contemporaneous record, and on the testimony of David L. Van Bebber, a lawyer involved in the Culinary acquisition, who believed that the underlying invoices were for the purchase, installation, or moving of equipment for the new processing facility on Ashland Avenue.

The Commissioner challenged Tyson's claim on strict statutory and evidentiary grounds. Respondent asserted, citing INDOPCO, Inc. v. Commissioner, 503 U.S. 79, 84 (1992), that deductions are a matter of legislative grace and that the taxpayer must clearly demonstrate entitlement to any deductions claimed, even capital deductions, and the Court confirmed that Tyson bore the burden of proving entitlement under Tax Court Rule 142(a). Under I.R.C. § 6001 and Treas. Reg. § 1.6001-1, every taxpayer is legally obligated to keep permanent books of account or records, including inventories and source invoices, sufficient to establish the amount of gross income, deductions, credits, or other matters required to be shown on any return. The Commissioner's primary criticism was that the list of expenditures on which Tyson relied covered the entire calendar year 1995 and could not be allocated to the fiscal years before the Court, and that it contained no information regarding the nature of each expense or when within 1995 it was incurred; Respondent added that Tyson had no evidence to substantiate its allegation that, merely because account No. 101226 was labeled "TIF Moving Expenses" and the TIF subsidy was given in connection with Culinary, all of the disputed amounts must represent moving expenses of food processing equipment capitalizable over five years. Respondent maintained that Tyson was asking the Court to make a "leap of faith" without any corroborating evidence that the remaining amounts were for the purchase, the installation, or the moving of equipment for use in Culinary's processing facility, and emphasized Tyson's status in the industry and its employment of in-house and outside accountants and tax preparers who were well aware of the recordkeeping requirements of the Internal Revenue Code.
Governing Statutory Framework and Judicial Precedent in R&D Tax Credit Jurisprudence

Although the immediate holding in T.C. Memo. 2007-188 adjudicated depreciation substantiation while the substantive I.R.C. § 41 issue in Docket No. 21590-03 remained deferred, Tyson Foods, Inc. v. Commissioner has been cited in subsequent United States R&D tax credit commentary and litigation. In the landmark R&D tax credit decision Union Carbide Corp. & Subsidiaries v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2009-50, aff'd, 697 F.3d 104 (2d Cir. 2012), the Tax Court explicitly cited Tyson Foods, Inc. & Subs. v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2007-188 alongside Boyd v. Commissioner, 122 T.C. 305, 320 (2004) and Eustace v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2001-66, aff'd, 312 F.3d 905 (7th Cir. 2002), to define the strict evidentiary boundaries of I.R.C. § 6001 and the Cohan rule when taxpayers attempt to estimate Qualified Research Expenses (QREs) under I.R.C. § 41. Similarly, a 2009 article in The Tax Adviser, the journal of the American Institute of Certified Public Accountants (AICPA), analyzing the proposed Statements on Standards for Tax Services (SSTS), discussed Tyson Foods under proposed SSTS No. 4 (Use of Estimates), alongside research credit disallowance rulings, as illustrating that estimates must be reasonable and rest on sufficient evidence rather than speculation.

In the United States federal tax system, the R&D tax credit is governed by a tightly interlocking statutory and regulatory architecture centered on I.R.C. § 41. Under I.R.C. § 41(a) and (b), Congress established an incremental tax credit equal to 20 percent of the excess of a taxpayer's QREs for the taxable year over a statutory base amount, alongside an alternative simplified credit calculation under I.R.C. § 41(c)(4) equal to 14 percent of QREs exceeding 50 percent of the average QREs for the three preceding taxable years. Statutory QREs are strictly confined to "in-house research expenses"—comprising wages paid or incurred for qualified services and amounts paid or incurred for supplies used in the conduct of qualified research—and "contract research expenses," which generally encompass 65 percent of amounts paid or incurred to third parties for the performance of qualified research on the taxpayer's behalf.

A critical statutory boundary exists under I.R.C. § 41(b)(2)(C) and I.R.C. §§ 167 and 168 regarding tangible property used in research and plant modernization. Section 41(b)(2)(C) defines creditable "supplies" as any tangible property other than land or improvements to land, and other than property of a character subject to the allowance for depreciation. This statutory exclusion creates a direct legal tension between capitalizable machinery and equipment—which must be depreciated over its recovery period under I.R.C. §§ 167 and 168—and consumable research supplies creditable under I.R.C. § 41(b)(2)(A)(ii). Consequently, establishing the exact physical and accounting character of plant and equipment expenditures—the precise factual domain at issue in Tyson Foods—is decisive for both capital recovery and R&D tax credit eligibility.

Furthermore, I.R.C. § 41(d) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4 mandate that for an activity to constitute "qualified research," the taxpayer must satisfy a cumulative Four-Part Test applied separately to each discrete "business component," defined as any product, process, computer software, technique, formula, or invention to be held for sale, lease, or license, or used by the taxpayer in a trade or business. First, under the Section 174 Test of I.R.C. § 41(d)(1)(A), expenditures must qualify as research and experimental expenditures under I.R.C. § 174, meaning they are incurred in connection with the taxpayer's trade or business and represent R&D costs in the experimental or laboratory sense aimed at eliminating uncertainty concerning the development or improvement of a product or process. Second, under the Technological in Nature Test of I.R.C. § 41(d)(1)(B)(i), the research must be undertaken for the purpose of discovering information that is technological in nature, relying fundamentally on principles of the physical or biological sciences, engineering, or computer science. Third, under the Permitted Purpose Test of I.R.C. § 41(d)(1)(B)(ii), the application of that discovered information must be intended to be useful in the development of a new or improved business component of the taxpayer relating to function, performance, reliability, or quality. Fourth, under the Process of Experimentation Test of I.R.C. § 41(d)(1)(C), substantially all—defined by regulation as at least 80 percent—of the research activities must constitute elements of a process of experimentation capable of evaluating one or more alternatives to achieve a result where the capability or method of achieving that result, or the appropriate design of that result, is uncertain as of the beginning of the taxpayer's research activities. Overarching this entire substantive framework is the recordkeeping mandate of I.R.C. § 6001, Treas. Reg. § 1.6001-1, and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(d), which obligates taxpayers to maintain sufficiently usable and detailed records to substantiate both the qualitative eligibility of the research activities and the quantitative nexus between accounting costs and qualified business components.
The Tax Court's Final Holding

In Tyson Foods, Inc. v. Commissioner, Judge Cohen ruled in favor of the Commissioner on this issue, holding that Tyson failed to satisfy its burden of proving that it was entitled to the disputed deductions, i.e., the additional $2,007,640 beyond the $1,800,354 reduction in income that Respondent had already conceded. The Court declined Tyson's invocation of the Cohan rule for two related reasons. First, the Court held that the record did not contain sufficient reliable evidence to provide a basis for making an estimate. While the Cohan doctrine permits the Tax Court to estimate the amount of an allowable deduction or credit when a taxpayer proves that a qualifying expenditure was incurred but cannot establish the exact dollar figure, the Court must have some factual basis in the record upon which to make a rational estimate. Because Tyson produced only a list of vendors and amounts recorded in the TIF moving expenses account—which was contemporaneous only with respect to the recording of amounts in that account, not in the sense that invoices, purchase orders, or journal entry explanations reflected the nature of the items purchased—together with a witness's speculation based on familiarity with certain vendors, and because no invoices were in the record or ever produced, the Court found no reliable evidence that the items paid for were deductible currently or over time through depreciation, or that the expenditures were attributable to a tax year before the Court; on a record in which erroneous accounting entries had been established, the Court had no confidence that the expenditures were for the purpose claimed. Second, the Court emphasized that approximations under the Cohan rule necessarily bear heavily upon taxpayers whose inexactitude in failing to keep records created the problem, while noting that this was not a case in which no allowance had been made for the costs of relocating the Culinary facility, since a substantial amount had been conceded by Respondent. The argument that Tyson's status in the industry and its employment of in-house and outside accountants and tax preparers "who were well aware of the record keeping requirements of the Internal Revenue Code" weighed against Tyson was advanced by Respondent; Judge Cohen recited that argument but did not expressly adopt a separate "sophisticated taxpayer" standard, resting the holding instead on the absence of reliable evidence and noting that the section 7491 burden shift is available only where the taxpayer has maintained all required records and, for corporations, only to those with a limited net worth, unlike Tyson.
Section 2: Core Legal & Evidentiary Failures

An exhaustive examination of Tyson Foods, Inc. v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2007-188, and its direct application in subsequent Tax Court R&D credit rulings such as Union Carbide Corp. v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2009-50, exposes four interconnected pillars of legal, technical, contractual, and documentation failure. When corporate taxpayers present R&D tax credit or capital cost recovery studies built upon top-down accounting reclassifications rather than bottom-up technical and financial records, these four failure modes consistently result in wholesale disallowance.
Collapse of Contemporaneous Documentation and General Ledger Reclassification Failures (I.R.C. § 6001)

The primary evidentiary failure in Tyson Foods was the taxpayer's attempt to substantiate $2,007,640 of claimed deductions—argued, at a minimum, to be capital expenditures depreciable over five years—solely through a list of vendors and amounts recorded in account No. 101226, designated "TIF moving expenses," and the testimony of a lawyer who admitted that he had not been involved in the accounting for the TIF subsidy or the disputed expenditures, without producing underlying source documents such as invoices, purchase orders, or journal entry explanations reflecting the nature of the items purchased. In corporate tax practice, this failure mirrors the classic defect in retroactive R&D tax credit studies, wherein tax advisors extract macro-level cost center balances, department-wide payroll registers, or trial balance accounts (such as "Plant Engineering," "Process Support," or "Moving and Trial Expenses") and apply arbitrary allocation percentages without linking specific expenditures to specific qualified activities.

Under I.R.C. § 6001 and Treas. Reg. § 1.6001-1(a), a taxpayer must keep permanent books of account or records, including inventories, as are sufficient to establish the amount of gross income, deductions, credits, or other matters required to be shown by such person in any return of such tax. As the Tax Court demonstrated in Tyson Foods, an accounting entry on a general ledger is not self-proving; it is merely an assertion by management of how an outlay was categorized for internal bookkeeping. Moreover, Tyson itself conceded that its records were insufficient to determine whether the disputed amounts should have reduced ordinary and necessary business expenses or depreciation, and the Court stressed that, on a record in which erroneous accounting entries had been established, it had no confidence that the expenditures were for the purpose claimed. Without primary source invoices showing exactly what was purchased, who performed the work, when the service occurred, and how the item functioned within an experimental or capital project, the Tax Court will not treat a ledger balance, a vendor list recorded under it, or a witness's speculation about it as reliable evidence of entitlement.
Fatal Misapplication of the Cohan Estimation Doctrine and the "Sophisticated Taxpayer" Penalty

For decades, corporate taxpayers defending aggressive I.R.C. § 41 R&D credit claims and capital recovery positions relied on Cohan v. Commissioner, 39 F.2d 540, 543–544 (2d Cir. 1930), as an evidentiary safety net. Under Cohan, if the trial record establishes that a taxpayer actually engaged in qualified research or incurred a deductible expense, but the taxpayer's records are inadequate to establish the exact dollar amount, the court may estimate the allowable amount, "bearing heavily if it chooses upon the taxpayer whose inexactitude is of his own making".

Tyson Foods illustrates the limits of reliance on Cohan through two considerations: the evidentiary-basis prerequisite applied by the Court and the institutional sophistication argument advanced by Respondent. Under the evidentiary-basis prerequisite, as stated in Tyson Foods (citing Mendes v. Commissioner, 121 T.C. 308 (2003), and Vanicek v. Commissioner, 85 T.C. 731, 742-743 (1985)), a court may invoke Cohan to estimate allowable deductions only when it is clear that deductible expenses have been incurred, and there must be sufficient evidence in the record to provide a basis for making an estimate. In Tyson Foods, because no invoices were in the record or ever produced, the vendor list did not identify the nature of the items or the dates on which they were expended, and the witness's testimony was speculation, Tyson failed to prove that the disputed $2,007,640 was deductible currently or over time through depreciation, or that the expenditures were attributable to a tax year before the Court. When the Tax Court later applied Tyson Foods in Union Carbide Corp. v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2009-50, it held that while Cohan can be used to estimate qualified research wages or costs once a specific project and a specific employee's direct participation in a process of experimentation are proven on the record, Cohan cannot be used to bridge a failure to prove that qualified research occurred or to validate uncorroborated, speculative estimates lacking a rational basis.

Compounding this evidentiary barrier is the institutional sophistication argument advanced by Respondent and recited by Judge Cohen. Respondent emphasized Tyson's status in the industry and its employment of in-house and outside accountants and tax preparers who were well aware of the recordkeeping requirements of the Internal Revenue Code; the Court did not expressly adopt this as a separate holding, but it reiterated that approximations under the Cohan rule bear heavily upon taxpayers whose inexactitude in failing to keep records created the problem, and it noted that the section 7491 burden shift is available only to taxpayers that have maintained all required records (and, for corporations, only to those with a limited net worth, unlike Tyson). On the logic of Respondent's argument, unlike an unsophisticated individual proprietor who inadvertently misplaces receipts, a major enterprise equipped with enterprise resource planning (ERP) systems and professional tax counsel possesses both the legal duty and the institutional capability to maintain granular project accounting. When such a taxpayer fails to preserve primary documentation—as Tyson failed to do for the disputed 1995 expenditures recorded after its August 1994 purchase of Culinary—the Tax Court will not treat the evidentiary gap as an excusable oversight warranting estimation where, as in Tyson Foods, the record provides no reliable basis for an estimate.
Technical Eligibility Deficiencies: Uncertainty, Process of Experimentation, and Nexus to the Business Component

When the evidentiary standards of Tyson Foods are applied to substantive R&D tax credit claims—the research credit issue in Docket No. 21590-03 itself was deferred and was not addressed in T.C. Memo. 2007-188, but comparable standards appear in Union Carbide and Eustace—taxpayers routinely fail to establish the technical elements of the I.R.C. § 41(d) Four-Part Test because their documentation does not link cost pools to specific business components. Under I.R.C. § 174 and Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)(1), uncertainty exists only if the information available to the taxpayer does not establish the capability or method for developing or improving the product or process, or the appropriate design of the product or process. In industrial food processing and manufacturing environments generally (the Tyson Foods opinion itself made no findings on technological uncertainty), taxpayers frequently conflate engineering logistics, plant layout optimization, equipment relocation, and routine calibration with true technological uncertainty. Moving a production line, integrating acquired machinery into a new facility, or adjusting conveyor speeds using known mechanical engineering parameters resolves operational or project management uncertainty rather than technological uncertainty.

Even where genuine technological uncertainty exists at the outset of a project, taxpayers frequently fail to demonstrate a structured process of experimentation under I.R.C. § 41(d)(1)(C). As emphasized in Eustace v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2001-66, which was cited alongside Tyson Foods in Union Carbide, a process of experimentation requires a systematic, scientific evaluation of one or more alternatives—through modeling, simulation, systematic trial and error, or hypothesis formulation and testing—where the outcome is uncertain at the outset. Ad hoc trial runs on a commercial processing line or routine troubleshooting during equipment commissioning do not satisfy the "substantially all" (80 percent) threshold of I.R.C. § 41(d)(1)(C) unless the taxpayer documents the scientific hypotheses tested, the specific technical variables isolated, and the empirical data comparing alternative designs.

Furthermore, under the "shrinking-back rule" of Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(b)(2), if an overall plant modification or commercial production line fails the Four-Part Test as a whole, the test must be applied to the most significant subset of elements—such as a specific thermal pasteurization sub-assembly or a novel polymer catalyst injector—that actually entails technological uncertainty. Under the Tyson Foods and Boyd substantiation standard, if a taxpayer aggregates all plant modification or engineering costs into a single macro-account without tracking labor hours, supplies, and equipment usage down to the specific qualifying sub-component, the Court may be unable to apply the shrinking-back rule and may disallow the entire cost pool.
Production-Scale Supply Boundaries, Depreciable Property Exclusions, and Contractual/M&A Pitfalls

The intersection of Tyson Foods and Union Carbide highlights acute legal vulnerabilities surrounding physical assets, commercial production trials, and corporate contracts. Under I.R.C. § 41(b)(2)(C), property of a character subject to the allowance for depreciation is strictly excluded from qualifying as a "supply" QRE. Conversely, to depreciate an asset under I.R.C. §§ 167 and 168, the taxpayer must prove its capital character, placed-in-service date, and cost basis. In TG Missouri Corp. v. Commissioner, 133 T.C. 278 (2009), a case frequently analyzed alongside Tyson Foods in R&D tax controversy literature, the Tax Court examined the precise legal boundary between depreciable production molds sold to customers and supplies eligible for the research credit under I.R.C. § 41(b)(2)(C). When a taxpayer fails to preserve vendor invoices and technical specifications during plant upgrades—as Tyson failed to produce invoices for the disputed $2,007,640 debited to Culinary's TIF moving expenses account—it falls into a fatal substantiation whipsaw: the expenditure lacks the capital asset documentation required for depreciation under I.R.C. § 167, yet simultaneously lacks the consumable material documentation and experimental nexus required to qualify as a supply QRE under I.R.C. § 41(b)(2)(A)(ii).

A closely related pitfall arises when taxpayers claim raw materials consumed during plant-based commercial trial runs. As illustrated in Union Carbide Corp. v. Commissioner, where the Tax Court cited Tyson Foods in evaluating plant-based process R&D claims, when a manufacturer conducts process experimentation on commercial production equipment while manufacturing goods for sale, the IRS and the courts disallow the cost of raw materials and routine plant supplies that the taxpayer "would have incurred regardless of any qualified research it was conducting". Under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(b)(1), such routine raw material inputs are treated as excluded "indirect research expenditures" rather than supplies used in the direct conduct of qualified research.

Finally, the record in Tyson Foods shows that Tyson's substantiation problem arose from post-acquisition accounting errors: no part of the August 1994 purchase price was initially allocated to the TIF subsidy receivable, and the City of Chicago's subsidy payments were later credited to land, goodwill, TIF moving expenses, and miscellaneous other income accounts rather than to a receivable. In corporate acquisitions and third-party engineering engagements, failure to retain executed vendor contracts, statements of work (SOWs), and itemized invoices is doubly fatal. For R&D tax credits, I.R.C. § 41(d)(4)(H) excludes any research to the extent it is "funded" by any grant, contract, or otherwise by another person, including municipal incentives, customer reimbursements, or original equipment manufacturer (OEM) cost-sharing. Moreover, under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(e), payments to third-party engineering contractors qualify as contract research expenses only if the agreement is entered into prior to the performance of the qualified research, requires the research to be performed on behalf of the taxpayer, and requires the taxpayer to bear the financial risk of failure while retaining substantial rights in the research results. Without the underlying contracts and invoices—as occurred with the never-produced invoices and the TIF subsidy receivable whose payments were misapplied in Tyson Foods—a taxpayer cannot establish contractual risk, intellectual property ownership, or cost basis.

body.text: Section 4: Two Applied Remedial Case Studies

To translate the judicial holdings of Tyson Foods, Inc. v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2007-188, and its R&D tax credit progeny into actionable corporate compliance architectures, the following two applied case studies examine realistic industrial scenarios facing the exact legal, technical, contractual, and accounting pitfalls identified by the Tax Court. Each case study provides a step-by-step remedial blueprint covering project governance, technical documentation, contract drafting, and financial experimentation tracking.
Case Study 1: Automated Poultry & Food Processing Facility Modernization (Post-Acquisition Plant Integration, Equipment Scale-Up, and Process Experimentation)
Scenario and Vulnerability Profile

Apex Protein Corp. (Apex), a publicly traded United States food manufacturer employing an internal tax department and Big Four auditors, acquires 100 percent of the stock of Gourmet Poultry Inc. (Gourmet) for $85 million. Immediately following the acquisition, Apex initiates "Project Phoenix," a $4.5 million initiative at Gourmet's Midwest facility to consolidate two legacy processing lines and develop a novel, high-speed automated cryogenic crust-freezing and high-pressure processing (HPP) pathogen-lethality system for ready-to-eat poultry fillets. During the 14-month project, Gourmet's accounting staff books $2.8 million of vendor payments, engineering contractor bills, equipment rigging costs, and prototype fabrication outlays into a single general ledger clearing account labeled GL #64500 (Plant Consolidation & Moving Expenses). An additional $1.7 million in internal plant engineering wages and raw poultry test batches is recorded in GL #51200 (Plant Operations Overhead). Due to post-merger ERP migration from Gourmet's legacy software to Apex's SAP instance, physical vendor invoices and contractor work orders for GL #64500 are boxed and lost. On its consolidated federal return, Apex claims I.R.C. § 41 R&D tax credits on 50 percent of both accounts based on retrospective oral interviews with the plant manager, and claims I.R.C. § 168 Modified Accelerated Cost Recovery System (MACRS) depreciation on the remaining 50 percent of GL #64500.

Under Tyson Foods, Inc. v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2007-188, Apex's tax return position is fatally defective across every legal dimension. First, the general ledger designation "Plant Consolidation & Moving Expenses" directly contradicts both the capital asset character required for I.R.C. § 168 depreciation and the experimental character required for I.R.C. § 41 QREs. Second, because Apex lost the underlying invoices during the post-acquisition ERP transition, it stands in direct violation of the permanent recordkeeping mandate of I.R.C. § 6001. Third, as a publicly traded industry leader employing in-house and external CPAs, Apex would face the institutional-sophistication argument that Respondent advanced in Tyson Foods and the principle, reiterated by Judge Cohen, that Cohan approximations bear heavily on taxpayers whose own inexactitude created the problem; the Tax Court is likely to refuse to apply the Cohan rule to estimate either depreciable basis or R&D QREs from uncorroborated oral estimates and lump-sum ledger balances. Finally, commingling routine physical moving and rigging expenses with experimental HPP pathogen-lethality engineering violates the business-component nexus mandate of Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(b)(2) and the depreciable property exclusion of I.R.C. § 41(b)(2)(C).
Step 1: Restructuring Project Governance Through M&A Tax Integration and Stage-Gate Controls

To overcome the Tyson Foods evidentiary bar, Apex must first overhaul its corporate project governance and M&A integration protocols. Prior to closing any stock or asset acquisition, Apex's corporate tax department must issue a formal Tax Record Hold and ERP Migration Directive. Under this directive, all target company accounts payable ledgers, fixed asset sub-ledgers, vendor invoices, engineering change orders (ECOs), and municipal grant agreements must be digitized, verified for legibility, and indexed in an immutable enterprise document repository before legacy accounting systems are decommissioned.

Concurrently, Apex must institute a formal Stage-Gate R&D and Capital Expenditure Review Committee comprising the Vice President of Food Safety and Engineering, the Plant Controller, and Senior Tax Counsel. Before any capital authorization request (CAR) or project code is opened in SAP, the committee must segregate Project Phoenix into discrete "Business Components" under I.R.C. § 41(d)(2)(B) and non-qualifying operational sub-projects. Specifically, the committee must bifurcate Project Phoenix into three strict Work Breakdown Structure (WBS) codes: WBS-101 (Operational Moving & Rigging), capturing the disassembly, transport, and floor bolting of unchanged legacy conveyors deductible under I.R.C. § 162; WBS-102 (Capital Equipment Acquisition), capturing the purchase and standard installation of commercial-grade refrigeration compressors and structural mezzanines depreciable under I.R.C. §§ 167 and 168; and WBS-103 (Qualified Research Business Component), isolating the design, fluid-dynamic modeling, prototype fabrication, and microbial lethality testing of the novel Dual-Zone Cryogenic-HPP Chamber Sub-Assembly under I.R.C. §§ 41 and 174.
Step 2: Restructuring Technical Documentation to Satisfy the Four-Part Test

To eliminate the evidentiary vacuum criticized in Tyson Foods and Union Carbide, the engineering team assigned to WBS-103 must generate and archive contemporaneous technical artifacts mapped to each element of I.R.C. § 41(d). Prior to fabrication, the Lead Food Process Engineer must author a formal Technical Uncertainty Memorandum under I.R.C. § 174 documenting why existing engineering knowledge and off-the-shelf equipment cannot achieve a reduction in Listeria monocytogenes and Salmonella spp. within a 45-second residence time without inducing protein denaturation or surface freezer burn in raw poultry fillets. This memorandum explicitly distinguishes the scientific and thermodynamic design uncertainty of the chamber from the logistical task of moving plant lines.

As experimental work proceeds under WBS-103, engineers must record every iterative design alternative in a centralized Laboratory Information Management System (LIMS) and computer-aided design (CAD) version-control repository to prove a structured process of experimentation under I.R.C. § 41(d)(1)(C). For example, the LIMS dossier must document Hypothesis 1—evaluating impingement liquid nitrogen spray at followed by hydrostatic pressure for 30 seconds—against Hypothesis 2, which evaluates counter-current snow-horn pre-chilling at coupled with pulsed pressure waves. The technical file must preserve dated microbial assay reports, shear-force texture analyzer outputs, and computational fluid dynamics (CFD) thermal profiles demonstrating why Hypothesis 1 caused cellular fracturing and was rejected, and how iterative nozzle angle modifications in Hypothesis 2 resolved the uncertainty.
Step 3: Restructuring Contract Terms for Vendors, Fabricators, and Municipal Grants

To cure the missing-invoice and contract-ambiguity defects highlighted in Tyson Foods, Apex must revise its procurement and legal contracting standards. All Master Service Agreements (MSAs) with mechanical fabricators, electrical integrators, and rigging companies must strictly prohibit lump-sum billing such as "Plant Consolidation Services - $500,000". Instead, vendors must be contractually obligated to submit itemized line-item invoices referencing specific WBS codes (WBS-101, WBS-102, or WBS-103), specific CAD drawing numbers, labor hours by engineering classification, and exact bill-of-materials (BOM) part descriptions.

For third-party food scientists and specialized fluid-dynamics consultants working on WBS-103, executed SOWs must be signed prior to the commencement of work in strict compliance with Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(e). Each SOW must explicitly stipulate that the research is performed on behalf of Apex to resolve the defined technical uncertainties of WBS-103, that Apex retains exclusive title and substantial rights to all resulting patents, trade secrets, and engineering designs without royalty obligations, and that payment is billed on a time-and-materials basis rather than guaranteed technical performance, thereby placing the financial risk of failure squarely on Apex. Furthermore, if the local municipality provides a $300,000 economic development relocation grant—analogous to the city payment accounting issue noted in Tyson Foods—the grant agreement and internal accounting entries must explicitly allocate 100 percent of the municipal reimbursement to WBS-101 (non-R&D moving expenses) and establish a dedicated receivable sub-ledger so that no portion of WBS-103 QREs is disqualified as "funded research" under I.R.C. § 41(d)(4)(H).
Step 4: Restructuring Experimentation and Financial Tracking in the ERP System

Finally, Apex must align its SAP financial tracking with the substantiation standards of I.R.C. § 6001 and Union Carbide. Retrospective annual percentage surveys must be replaced with mandatory weekly ERP timesheets for all engineers, food scientists, and technicians. Each time entry logged under WBS-103 must select a statutory qualification tag—Direct Experimentation, Direct Supervision, or Direct Support under I.R.C. § 41(b)(2)(B)—and include a contemporaneous narrative linking the hours to a specific test protocol, such as 14.5 hours dedicated to CAD redesign of the cryogenic injector manifold for Trial #4 under WBS-103.

Simultaneously, the accounting system must enforce a rigid separation between consumable prototype supplies and depreciable capital assets. Custom-milled stainless steel test nozzles, sacrificial pressure seals, and non-reusable thermocouples destroyed during destructive testing of WBS-103 must be booked to GL #54110 (Direct R&D Consumable Supplies - WBS-103) with attached vendor invoices and scrap-disposal certificates proving they are not depreciable property under I.R.C. § 41(b)(2)(C). Raw poultry fillets inoculated with surrogate pathogens or subjected to destructive shear-testing must be tracked via batch-ticket barcodes and booked to GL #54120 (Destructive Test Raw Materials - WBS-103), accompanied by United States Department of Agriculture (USDA) condemnation and rendering logs proving that none of the test meat was sold to consumers. Once the final commercial HPP vessel design is frozen and released for commercial production, all subsequent fabrication and installation costs must be closed out of WBS-103 and capitalized into WBS-102 with full invoice substantiation to support MACRS depreciation under I.R.C. § 168.

body.text: Case Study 2: Industrial Chemical & Polymer Manufacturing Process Optimization (Plant-Scale Catalyst Trials, Raw Material Supplies, and Multi-Vendor Engineering Contracts)
Scenario and Vulnerability Profile

Vanguard Petrochemicals Inc. (Vanguard), a large domestic specialty chemical producer, seeks to improve olefin cracking yield and suppress coking degradation inside two commercial cracking furnaces (Furnaces 8 and 9) at its Gulf Coast refinery. Vanguard initiates the "Ultra-Yield Inhibitor Initiative," conducting 18 full-scale experimental trial runs directly on Furnaces 8 and 9 over a 10-month period while those furnaces continue to manufacture commercial-grade ethylene that is sold to downstream customers. To execute the project, Vanguard utilizes internal chemical engineers, purchases $6.2 million of hydrocarbon naphtha feedstock and $180,000 of experimental organometallic anticoking inhibitors, and pays $950,000 to an external engineering affiliate, ProcessTech LLC, which submits unitemized monthly lump-sum invoices stating "Monthly Technical & Plant Support Services". Vanguard maintains no contemporaneous log distinguishing routine furnace operating hours from experimental run hours. At tax return preparation, Vanguard's outside R&D tax consultant claims all $6.2 million of naphtha feedstock consumed during the 18 trial runs as qualified "supplies" under I.R.C. § 41(b)(2)(A)(ii), claims 65 percent of the $950,000 lump-sum ProcessTech invoices as contract research expenses, and claims an estimated 40 percent of all refinery operator and chemical engineer wages, invoking the Cohan rule to bridge the lack of time records.

This scenario directly replicates the fatal legal and evidentiary flaws adjudicated in Union Carbide Corp. v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2009-50, where the Tax Court explicitly relied upon Tyson Foods, Inc. v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2007-188. First, under Union Carbide and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(b)(1), the $6.2 million of naphtha feedstock used to manufacture commercial ethylene sold to customers will be disallowed in full because those raw material costs "would have been incurred regardless of any qualified research" Vanguard was conducting, rendering them excluded indirect research expenditures. Second, citing Tyson Foods, Boyd, and Eustace, the Tax Court will reject Vanguard's 40 percent across-the-board wage estimate and the unitemized ProcessTech monthly invoices. Because Vanguard is a sophisticated corporate taxpayer with established accounting personnel—the type of argument Respondent pressed in Tyson Foods—and because the record would provide no reliable basis for an estimate, the Court is likely to refuse to speculate under Cohan as to which refinery operators or ProcessTech contractors performed qualified experimental activities versus routine commercial plant operations.
Step 1: Restructuring Project Governance to Segregate Experimental Runs from Commercial Production

To establish an audit-proof boundary between commercial manufacturing and qualified process research, Vanguard must institute a formal Plant-Trial Authorization Protocol (PTAP) governed jointly by the Vice President of Process R&D and the Refinery Controller. Before any experimental run is conducted on a commercial furnace or reactor, the engineering and accounting teams must execute a numbered PTAP authorization defining the exact start timestamp and end timestamp of the experimental window, the specific furnace unit (such as Furnace 8, Coil Bank B), and the baseline steady-state operating parameters from which the experiment will deviate.

Furthermore, Vanguard's governance charter must enforce a "Pilot-Plant First" rule coupled with incremental run accounting. Wherever technically feasible, initial catalyst and inhibitor screening must be conducted in a dedicated non-commercial pilot reactor (isolated in Cost Center #8800 - Pilot R&D Lab) where 100 percent of feedstocks and outputs are flared or recycled rather than sold. When scale-up to commercial Furnaces 8 and 9 is technologically necessary because fluid-dynamic coking kinetics cannot be accurately modeled at pilot scale, project governance rules must restrict QRE capture strictly to the incremental experimental inputs and dedicated R&D personnel directly executing the authorized PTAP.
Step 2: Restructuring Technical Documentation to Isolate the Process of Experimentation

For each of the 18 furnace trials authorized under a PTAP, the Lead Chemical Engineer must compile a contemporaneous Pre-Run Scientific Hypothesis and Uncertainty Dossier in the company's Electronic Lab Notebook (ELN). This dossier must articulate the exact technological uncertainty under I.R.C. § 174—specifically, whether injecting a novel phosphorus-silicon organometallic inhibitor at concentrations between and at coil skin temperatures exceeding will passivate nickel catalytic sites on the inner radiant tube wall without poisoning downstream hydrogenation catalysts. The ELN must also set forth the matrix of experimental alternatives evaluated across Runs 1 through 18, detailing variations in inhibitor molecular formulations (Formulations A, B, and C), injection port geometries, and steam-to-hydrocarbon dilution ratios.

During each trial run, Vanguard must extract and archive raw, time-stamped Distributed Control System (DCS) telemetry—including pyrometer tube-skin temperatures, pressure drop () across the radiant coil, and gas chromatography effluent yields—directly into the PTAP technical file. Immediately following each run, the engineering team must author a formal Post-Run Engineering Evaluation Report comparing empirical run performance against the baseline control furnace, and retaining root-cause failure analyses for any runs aborted due to thermal spikes or off-specification product.
Step 3: Restructuring Contract Terms with Third-Party Engineering Affiliates and Chemical Suppliers

To cure the invoicing and substantiation defects identified in Tyson Foods and Union Carbide, Vanguard must overhaul its contractual arrangements with ProcessTech LLC and its specialty chemical vendors. Vanguard must terminate the single lump-sum monthly retainer arrangement ("Monthly Technical & Plant Support Services") and replace it with two legally distinct contracts executed prior to the tax year. Agreement 1 (Routine Plant Maintenance & Operations Support MSA) will govern routine refinery turnarounds, safety inspections, and commercial process monitoring, all of which are excluded from QREs. Agreement 2 (Master R&D Engineering Contract) must be drafted in strict conformity with Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(e): it must be executed prior to the performance of any trial run, specify that ProcessTech engineers are retained to design, instrument, and analyze the PTAP anticoking trials on Vanguard's behalf, stipulate that Vanguard bears full financial risk if the inhibitor trials fail or damage furnace coils, and vest 100 percent of intellectual property rights in Vanguard. Crucially, Agreement 2 must mandate that every monthly invoice attach daily contractor timesheets identifying the specific engineer's name, date, PTAP Run ID, and exact experimental task performed.

Similarly, purchase orders and supply contracts with specialty chemical manufacturers for the $180,000 of experimental organometallic anticoking inhibitors must be restructured to provide unambiguous source documentation under I.R.C. § 6001. Each vendor invoice must explicitly list the experimental compound batch numbers, state that the compounds were custom-synthesized or supplied specifically for PTAP experimental trials, and cross-reference the corresponding PTAP Run ID.
Step 4: Restructuring Experimentation and Financial Tracking to Avoid the Supply and Cohan Traps

In configuring its general ledger and payroll tracking systems, Vanguard must implement strict accounting controls that respect the holdings of Union Carbide and Tyson Foods. First, regarding supply QREs, Vanguard must exclude the $6.2 million of standard hydrocarbon naphtha feedstock that is converted into salable ethylene and sold to customers, as those feedstocks represent costs Vanguard would have incurred regardless of the research under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(b)(1). Conversely, Vanguard must isolate the $180,000 of experimental organometallic anticoking inhibitors, specialized tracer gases, and sacrificial gas-chromatography columns in a dedicated account, GL #52900 (Direct Process R&D Supplies - PTAP Tracked), supported by itemized vendor invoices and material injection logs. Additionally, if a specific experimental run (such as Run #7) intentionally pushes thermal parameters beyond commercial tolerances and produces off-specification pyrolysis gas that cannot be sold and must be destroyed, Vanguard must document the exact volume flared via certified flare-meter logs and capture only the raw material cost of that destroyed, non-salable batch as a direct research supply.

Second, regarding wage QREs, Vanguard must abandon the 40 percent blanket estimate that would be summarily disallowed under Tyson Foods. Dedicated R&D chemical engineers must record their hours contemporaneously via project timecards mapped to specific PTAP Run IDs. Because commercial refinery control-room operators primarily perform routine production monitoring excluded under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(c)(3), their base wages must be excluded from the R&D claim. Vanguard may capture operator wages only for specific, logged overtime or dedicated shift hours where an operator is pulled off routine commercial duties to manually calibrate experimental inhibitor injection pumps or collect manual effluent samples under the direct supervision of the Lead R&D Engineer during an active PTAP window, corroborated by signed and timestamped control-room shift logs.

body.text: Section 5: Strategic Conclusions for Corporate Tax Governance

The United States Tax Court's ruling in Tyson Foods, Inc. & Subsidiaries v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2007-188, and its subsequent integration into the fabric of I.R.C. § 41 R&D tax credit case law via Union Carbide Corp. v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2009-50, established an uncompromising evidentiary paradigm for corporate taxpayers. First, the decision illustrates the narrow availability of Cohan estimation for sophisticated enterprises lacking primary records: the Court reaffirmed that Cohan permits estimation only where it is clear that deductible expenses were incurred and the record supplies a basis for the estimate. Large and mid-market corporate taxpayers that employ internal accounting personnel, modern ERP systems, and external tax advisors can no longer rely on the Cohan rule to rescue unsubstantiated R&D tax credit or capital recovery claims; rather, the Commissioner can be expected to press a corporate taxpayer's institutional sophistication and familiarity with I.R.C. § 6001 against it, as Respondent did in Tyson Foods, and any approximation will bear heavily on a taxpayer whose own recordkeeping failures created the gap.

Second, Tyson Foods demonstrates that an account label, and a vendor list recorded under it, will not by itself establish the nature of the underlying expenditures in federal tax litigation. Summary accounting entries—whether labeled "moving expenses," "plant engineering," or "technical support"—cannot sustain a deduction or credit without underlying primary documentation, including itemized vendor invoices, executed pre-research contracts, contemporaneous timecards, and empirical engineering test logs, that proves both the statutory nature of the activity and its exact financial nexus to a qualified business component or capital asset. Because evidentiary failures frequently originate during corporate acquisitions, plant relocations, and commercial-scale production trials, corporate tax departments must embed I.R.C. § 6001 document-retention holds and project-level WBS accounting directly into M&A integration playbooks and plant engineering workflows before expenditures are incurred.
